etymology: From Old English feld, open country, level ground — the flat land as distinguished from the wooded and from the walled. The Hebrew sādeh carries the same contrast: it is what lies outside the city, outside the tent, outside the enclosure. This is why so much of Scripture's decisive action happens in the field. The field is where a man is unwatched, where the beast is wild, where the labour is done, and where there is no one to hear a cry.
biblical_def: The field is the open ground given to man for labour, and it is one of the plainest instruments of biblical theology. It is first the place of the curse: cursed is the ground for thy sake, thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth, and in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread. It is next the place of the first murder — Cain talked with Abel his brother, and when they were in the field Cain rose up against him — the field being precisely where there was no witness but God, whose answer was that the voice of his brother's blood cried from the ground. It is the place of providence toward the poor, since the law commanded that the corners of the field not be reaped and the gleanings not be gathered, which is how Ruth came to glean in the field belonging unto Boaz (Rut 2:3), and how a foreign widow was brought into the line of David and of Christ. It is the place of trust, for the lilies of the field neither toil nor spin and yet are clothed beyond Solomon. And in the Lord's own interpretation it becomes the world itself: “The field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; but the tares are the children of the wicked one” (Mat 13:38). To that He adds the harvest urgency — lift up your eyes, and look on the fields, for they are white already to harvest (Joh 4:35).
webster_summary: The open ground outside the city and the enclosure, given to man for labour under the curse; in Scripture the place of the first murder, of gleaning mercy to the poor, of the tares among the wheat, and, in the Lord's own exposition, a figure of the world itself.
webster_full: FIELD, n. 1. A piece of land inclosed for tillage or pasture; any part of the open country not covered with wood.
2. In Scripture, the open country, as opposed to the city and the tent. The beasts of the field; the herbs of the field; Cain and Abel were in the field. Genesis 4.
3. Ground appropriated to a crop, and hence a figure of the world in which the gospel is sown. The field is the world. Matt. 13.
4. The place of battle. The field of blood; to take the field; to keep the field. Hence also the plain of Megiddo and the valley of decision.
5. In the Mosaic law, the corners of the field and the gleanings were to be left for the poor and the stranger. Levit. 19; Ruth 2.
scriptures: Matthew 13:38
The field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; but the tares are the children of the wicked one;
Ruth 2:3
And she went, and came, and gleaned in the field after the reapers: and her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz, who was of the kindred of Elimelech.
John 4:35
Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest.
Isaiah 5:2

And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes.
corruption_summary: The parable of the field and the tares is regularly turned into a counsel of indifference — let everything grow, judge nothing — when the Lord's point is that final separation is certain and belongs to Him, not that difference is unreal.
corruption_paragraphs: Mat 13 is one of the most misapplied passages in the New Testament. Because the householder says, Let both grow together until the harvest, the parable is enlisted to forbid the church from marking any difference between the faithful and the false, and to make all discernment presumptuous. But the field in the parable is explicitly the world, not the church, and the Lord who forbids the servants to pull tares is the same Lord who commands the church to put away from among itself the wicked person, and who writes to Thyatira in anger because she suffered a false teacher to teach. The parable restrains vigilante uprooting in the world; it does not abolish discipline in the congregation. And its conclusion is anything but indifferent: the tares are gathered and burned, and the righteous shine forth as the sun.

A second corruption is agricultural and moral at once. The gleaning laws are read as an early welfare programme and then either dismissed as obsolete or annexed to a political scheme. What they actually establish is a particular kind of mercy: the owner does not harvest to the edge, and the poor must still come and glean. The provision is real, it costs the owner, and it preserves the labour and dignity of the one receiving. Ruth is not handed a portion; she works in the field from morning until evening, and Boaz commands that handfuls be let fall on purpose for her. The law is neither the modern entitlement nor the modern indifference, and it is worth recovering as it stands.
roots_summary: Hebrew sādeh is the open ground, the country outside the walls. Greek agros is the field or farm, and chōra the wider region, used of the fields white to harvest.
roots_lines: Hebrew sādeh (H7704) — field, open country; some 333 occurrences, from the beast of the field to the field of Machpelah that Abraham bought for a burying place.
Hebrew chēlqâh (H2513) — a portion or parcel of ground; the word for Naboth's inherited plot and for the parcel of a field that Jacob bought at Shechem.
Greek agros (G68) — a field, a farm, the country; the word of the field bought with the price of blood (Mat 27:7) and of the treasure hid in a field.
Greek chōra (G5561) — a region, a tract of country; used in Joh 4:35 of the fields white already to harvest.
Greek zizanion (G2215) — tares, darnel; a weed that closely resembles wheat until the ear forms, which is exactly why the householder forbids early uprooting.
usage: Of the open country under the curse: thorns and thistles (Gen 3:18); the beasts of the field; Cain and Abel in the field (Gen 4:8).
Of provision and gleaning: the corners of the field left unreaped (Lev 19:9); Ruth gleaning after the reapers (Rut 2:3).
Figuratively of the world and the harvest: the field is the world (Mat 13:38); the fields white already to harvest (Joh 4:35); the vineyard of the LORD of hosts (Isa 5:7).

etymology: From Old English weall, borrowed early from Latin vallum, a rampart or palisade — the military sense is the original one. Hebrew distinguishes what English does not: chōmâh is the city wall, the defensive circuit, while qīr is the wall of a house or a room. Almost every theologically weighted use in Scripture is the first — the wall that makes a city a city, whose breach is its ruin and whose rebuilding is its restoration.
biblical_def: The wall in Scripture is defence, identity, and separation together. A city without walls is the standing figure of defencelessness — he that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls. So the wall becomes the natural emblem of salvation: “We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks” (Isa 26:1), where the defence is not masonry but God's own saving act. Jericho's wall is the counter-instance, where God brings down what men trusted: the people shouted, and the wall fell down flat (Jos 6:20), taken not by engineering but by obedience and a trumpet. The rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah is the great narrative of the theme — “come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach” (Neh 2:17) — a work of prayer, of organised labour, of a trowel in one hand and a weapon in the other, and of resisting mockery from without and discouragement from within. The New Testament then does something startling with the figure. The one wall Christ came to destroy is the wall between Jew and Gentile: He “hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us” (Eph 2:14), abolishing in His flesh the enmity, to make in Himself of twain one new man. And the last city needs no defence at all, though it has a great and high wall, because nothing that defileth shall ever enter it.
webster_summary: The defensive circuit that makes a city a city; in Scripture the emblem of salvation appointed by God, of a ruin that shames and a rebuilding that restores, and — in its one abolished form — of the partition between Jew and Gentile broken down in the flesh of Christ.
webster_full: WALL, n. 1. A work or structure of stone, brick or other materials, raised to some height, and intended for a defense or security.
2. The side of a building, or of a room; in the Hebrew a distinct word from the wall of a city.
3. In Scripture, a defense, protection, or means of security. Salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks. Isa. 26. They were a wall unto us both by night and by day. 1 Sam. 25.
4. To take the wall; to take the upper or inner place, as of honor or precedence in a street.
5. Middle wall of partition; the barrier between Jew and Gentile, figured by the wall in the temple beyond which no stranger might pass, and broken down in Christ. Eph. 2.
scriptures: Nehemiah 2:17

Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.
Joshua 6:20

So the people shouted when the priests blew with the trumpets: and it came to pass, when the people heard the sound of the trumpet, and the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they took the city.
Isaiah 26:1
In that day shall this song be sung in the land of Judah; We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks.
Ephesians 2:14
For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;
corruption_summary: Eph 2:14 is pressed into service as a general principle that all boundaries are sinful, so that the one wall Christ abolished becomes an argument for abolishing every distinction Scripture actually keeps.
corruption_paragraphs: The middle wall of partition is a specific wall: the barrier in the temple beyond which no Gentile could pass on pain of death, and behind it the ceremonial law of circumcision, meats, and days that divided Jew from Gentile. Paul says Christ abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances, to make of twain one new man. That is a defined redemptive-historical claim, and it is complete. It is not a principle that every boundary is a wall and every wall is enmity. The same apostle who wrote Eph 2 also drew hard lines — between the church and the world, between sound doctrine and corrupt, between the Lord's table and the table of devils — and the same Bible that ends the Jew-Gentile partition also ends with a city whose wall is great and high and whose gate excludes whatsoever worketh abomination.

The practical damage of the misreading is that a church which believes all walls are enmity cannot practise discipline, guard its table, or maintain an ordained ministry, because each of these draws a line. Nehemiah is the corrective narrative. The rebuilding of the wall was not xenophobia; it was the recovery of a people who had been made a reproach because they had no defined life. And the opposition Nehemiah faced — ridicule first, then threat, then the offer of a friendly meeting in the plain of Ono — is the usual sequence faced by anyone who tries to rebuild what has been broken down. His answer stands: I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down.
roots_summary: Hebrew separates the city wall (chōmâh) from the house wall (qīr), and has a third word, gādēr, for the field hedge. Greek teichos is the city wall; mesotoichon, the middle wall, occurs once, in Eph 2:14.
roots_lines: Hebrew chōmâh (H2346) — a city wall, the defensive circuit; the wall of Jericho, the wall Nehemiah built, and the wall of the beloved in Son 8:9.
Hebrew qīr (H7023) — the wall of a house or chamber; the wall on which the writing appeared in Belshazzar's palace and the wall Hezekiah turned his face to in prayer.
Hebrew gādēr (H1447) — a hedge or fence about a field or vineyard; whence the hedge God set about Job, and the breaking down of the hedge in Psa 80:12.
Greek teichos (G5038) — a city wall; used of Paul let down by the wall in a basket (Act 9:25) and of the great and high wall of the new Jerusalem.
Greek mesotoichon (G3320) — a middle wall, a dividing partition; a single New Testament occurrence, Eph 2:14, and the whole doctrine of Jew-Gentile union hangs on it.
usage: Of defence and its loss: a city that is broken down, and without walls (Pro 25:28); they were a wall unto us both by night and by day (1Sa 25:16).
Of God as the true defence: salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks (Isa 26:1); I will be unto her a wall of fire round about (Zec 2:5).
Of the partition abolished: the middle wall of partition broken down (Eph 2:14), making of twain one new man, so making peace.

etymology: From Old French tur, from Latin turris, a high structure. The Hebrew migdāl comes from gādal, to be great, to grow, to magnify — a tower is literally a greatening, a made-tall thing. That etymology is the whole moral history of the tower in Scripture, because the same root that builds a refuge builds a boast, and the difference between the two is whose name is on it.
biblical_def: Scripture sets two towers against each other and the contrast is exact. At Babel men said, “Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name” (Gen 11:4) — a tower built upward out of fear of being scattered, and built expressly to secure a name for the builders. The LORD came down to see the city and the tower which the children of men builded, and the making of a name ended in the confusion of speech. Over against it stands Solomon's proverb: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10). The one tower is climbed to make a name; the other is a name, and it is entered by running rather than built by labour. Between these lie the ordinary towers of the working world — the watchtower in the vineyard, built to guard fruit (Isa 5:2), and the tower of the parable whose builder must sit down first and count the cost, lest all that behold begin to mock him (Luk 14:28). That parable is the Lord's own warning against undertaking discipleship as a project of enthusiasm, and it stands directly beside the Babel account in sense: the man who builds without reckoning and the men who build to make a name both end mocked, and both end scattered from what they meant to raise.
webster_summary: A high structure raised for defence, watching, or display; in Scripture divided between the tower of Babel, built upward to make a name and ending in confusion, and the name of the LORD, which is a strong tower entered by the righteous who run into it.
webster_full: TOWER, n. 1. A building, either round or square, raised to a considerable elevation, and consisting of several stories.
2. A fortress; a citadel; a place of defense or of watching. Thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy. Psalm 61.
3. In Scripture, a figure of the divine protection. The name of the LORD is a strong tower. Prov. 18.
4. A watchtower in a vineyard or field, built for the keeper who guarded the fruit in the season. Isa. 5; Matt. 21.
5. The tower of Babel; the structure built in the plain of Shinar, whose top was to reach to heaven, and at which the language of the builders was confounded. Gen. 11.
scriptures: Genesis 11:4
And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.
Proverbs 18:10
The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
Luke 14:28
For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?
Nehemiah 2:17

Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.
corruption_summary: Babel is retold as a myth explaining language diversity, or admired as a symbol of human aspiration wrongly punished by a jealous God, when the text presents it as an act of self-naming judged in mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: The common academic handling treats Gen 11 as an aetiological legend composed to explain why nations speak differently — a story about language rather than an event with a judgment in it. This assumes what it should prove, namely that the early chapters of Genesis are not historical narrative. Moses writes them as history, with a place (a plain in the land of Shinar), a technology (brick for stone, and slime for morter), a stated motive (let us make us a name), and a consequence. The genealogy of Gen 10 already presumes the dispersion, and Gen 11 supplies its cause. The text is not accounting for a curiosity; it is recording a rebellion and its remedy.

The second and more flattering misreading admires the builders. Babel becomes the emblem of human aspiration, ambition, and unity, checked by a God who resents His creatures' reach. But Scripture nowhere condemns building, height, or skill; Bezaleel was filled with the Spirit of God for craftsmanship, and the temple was magnificent. What is condemned at Babel is the purpose — let us make us a name — which is the exact inversion of the promise God would shortly make to Abram: I will make thy name great. One name is seized and one is given. And the scattering was mercy, not spite: a united humanity in that condition would have been a greater tyranny, and the confusion of tongues that judged Babel was answered at Pentecost, when men of every nation heard the wonderful works of God each in his own language.
roots_summary: Hebrew migdāl, from gādal (to be great), names the tower as a made-great thing; it appears in place-names such as Migdal-el and in the tower of the flock, Migdal-eder. Greek purgos covers watchtower, fortress, and the tower of the parables.
roots_lines: Hebrew migdāl (H4026) — a tower, a raised platform; from gādal (H1431), to grow great, to magnify — the same root behind gedullah, greatness.
Hebrew 'ōphel (H6076) — a mound or stronghold, rendered tower in Isa 32:14 and used of the fortified rise in Jerusalem south of the temple.
Hebrew bābel (H894) — Babel, Babylon; the Babylonians derived it as the gate of god, but Moses ties it by sound to bālal (H1101), to confound.
Greek purgos (G4444) — a tower; used of the tower in the vineyard (Mat 21:33), the tower of Siloam that fell (Luk 13:4), and the tower of the counting-the-cost parable.
Greek onoma (G3686) — name; the word that carries the whole contrast, since Babel sought a name for itself and Pro 18:10 makes the name of the LORD the refuge.
usage: Of defence and refuge: a strong tower from the enemy (Psa 61:3); the name of the LORD is a strong tower (Pro 18:10).
Of watching over fruit and flock: he built a tower in the midst of it (Isa 5:2); the tower of the flock, Migdal-eder (Mic 4:8).
Of presumption and its judgment: a tower whose top may reach unto heaven (Gen 11:4); a builder who did not count the cost (Luk 14:28).

etymology: From Old French tente, from Latin tendere, to stretch — a tent is a stretched thing, a dwelling made of cloth pulled taut over poles. The Hebrew 'ōhel is the ordinary word for the black goat-hair dwelling of the patriarchs and of the wilderness camp, and it is also the word for the tabernacle, the tent of meeting. That single word doing both jobs is the doctrine: the God of Israel dwelt in the same kind of dwelling as His people, and moved when they moved.
biblical_def: The tent is the dwelling of the pilgrim, and Scripture makes it the mark of faith rather than of poverty. Abraham had wealth enough for a city and lived in a tent, “dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise”, for he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God (Heb 11:9-10). The tent is portable, provisional, and easily struck — which is precisely why the man who is waiting for a city can live in one contentedly. Lot furnishes the warning: he “pitched his tent toward Sodom” (Gen 13:12), and the pitching of a tent in a direction turns out to be the first step of a settlement that ends in fire. Balaam, hired to curse, looked on the camp and could only bless what he saw — “How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, and thy tabernacles, O Israel!” (Num 24:5). The tabernacle then takes the same form deliberately: God will not dwell in a house while His people dwell in tents, and He says so to David. The consummation of the figure is in John's prologue, where the Word made flesh tabernacled among us — the verb is the tent-word — and in Revelation, where the tabernacle of God is with men, and He shall dwell with them. Paul, a tentmaker by trade, uses the same figure for the body: our earthly house of this tabernacle shall be dissolved, and we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
webster_summary: The stretched cloth dwelling of the patriarchs and the wilderness camp; in Scripture the mark of the pilgrim who waits for a city with foundations, the form God chose for His own dwelling among a moving people, and Paul's figure for the mortal body.
webster_full: TENT, n. 1. A pavilion or portable lodge consisting of canvas or other coarse cloth, stretched and sustained by poles; used for sheltering persons from the weather.
2. In Scripture, the habitation of the patriarchs and of Israel in the wilderness. Abraham dwelt in tents with Isaac and Jacob. Heb. 11.
3. The tabernacle; the tent of the congregation, in which God was pleased to dwell among his people, and which was taken down and set up as they journeyed. Exod. 33.
4. Figuratively, the body, as the frail and temporary dwelling of the soul. Our earthly house of this tabernacle. 2 Cor. 5.
5. To pitch a tent; to fix and set up a tent for lodging. Lot pitched his tent toward Sodom. Gen. 13.
scriptures: Genesis 13:12
Abram dwelled in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, and pitched his tent toward Sodom.
Hebrews 11:9
By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise:
Numbers 24:5
How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, and thy tabernacles, O Israel!
Genesis 18:1
And the LORD appeared unto him in the plains of Mamre: and he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day;
corruption_summary: The pilgrim character of the Christian life is either dissolved into a spirituality that despises settled duty, or abandoned altogether for a religion of permanent comfort in which nothing is provisional.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors flank the tent. The first mistakes pilgrimage for rootlessness — a piety that treats every settled obligation as worldliness, and so declines to build, to plant, to marry, to join a congregation, or to bear the ordinary weight of a place. Scripture does not commend this. Jeremiah told the exiles in Babylon to build houses and dwell in them, plant gardens and eat the fruit of them, and seek the peace of the city. Abraham lived in a tent and still bought a field for a burying place, dug wells, and made covenants. The pilgrim does not refuse the land; he refuses to make it his hope.

The opposite and far commoner error is to lose the provisional altogether. Where a life is arranged on the assumption that this arrangement is final, the tent has become a house, and the loss shows up first in how loss is borne. Lot is the case study, and the text is precise about the sequence: he lifted up his eyes and saw the plain well watered, he chose it, he pitched his tent toward Sodom, and then he dwelt in Sodom, and then he sat in the gate of Sodom. No single step announces itself as apostasy. The remedy is not to strike the tent and wander, but to keep knowing that it is a tent — which is why Israel was commanded to keep the feast of tabernacles annually in booths, so that a settled generation should remember, once a year and in their bodies, what they were.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'ōhel serves both for the patriarch's tent and for the tent of meeting. Greek skēnē is the tent or tabernacle, and its verb skēnoō is what John uses of the Word made flesh dwelling among us.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ōhel (H168) — tent, tabernacle, dwelling; some 345 occurrences, covering both Abraham's tent and the tent of the congregation.
Hebrew mishkān (H4908) — a dwelling place, the tabernacle proper; from shākan, to settle down, dwell — the root behind the later term shekinah.
Hebrew succâh (H5521) — a booth of branches; the shelter of the feast of tabernacles, kept seven days so that generations should know that Israel dwelt in booths.
Greek skēnē (G4633) — a tent, tabernacle; used of the wilderness tabernacle in Heb 8-9 and of the true tabernacle which the Lord pitched, and not man.
Greek skēnoō (G4637) — to pitch a tent, to tabernacle; the verb of Joh 1:14, the Word dwelt among us, and of Rev 21:3, he shall dwell with them.
usage: Of patriarchal dwelling and pilgrimage: dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob (Heb 11:9); he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day (Gen 18:1).
Of the tabernacle as God's dwelling with a moving people: the tent of the congregation (Exo 33:7); the tabernacle of God is with men (Rev 21:3).
Of the body and its dissolution: our earthly house of this tabernacle (2Co 5:1); knowing that shortly I must put off this my tabernacle (2Pe 1:14).

etymology: From Old Norse vindauga, literally wind-eye — the opening through which the wind comes and through which the house sees. The compound is one of the most vivid survivals in English, and it happens to match the Hebrew usage closely, since 'arūbbâh means a lattice or sluice and is the word for the windows of heaven, openings through which what is above is poured down upon what is below.
biblical_def: The window in Scripture is an opening in a barrier, and its theology follows from that: it is the point at which what is outside comes in, or what is inside is let out. Heaven has windows, and they are opened for judgment and for blessing alike. At the flood “the windows of heaven were opened” (Gen 7:11), and the same phrase in Malachi becomes the great promise attached to the tithe: “prove me now herewith…if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it” (Mal 3:10). The window is also the way of escape for those under the protection of a promise. Rahab “let them down by a cord through the window” (Jos 2:15), and the scarlet line she was to bind in that same window became the mark that saved her house — a window that is at once the means of deliverance for the spies and the sign of deliverance for her family. Paul was let down by the wall in a basket through a window at Damascus. And a window can be the place of judgment: Jezebel looked out at a window and was cast down; Michal looked through a window and despised David in her heart; Eutychus “sat in a window…being fallen into a deep sleep” and fell to his death and was raised (Act 20:9). Daniel's windows are the most deliberate of all: knowing the writing was signed, he went into his house, his windows being open toward Jerusalem, and prayed as he did aforetime — open windows as a refusal to hide obedience.
webster_summary: An opening in a wall to admit light and air; in Scripture the aperture of heaven opened for flood or for blessing, the means of escape for Rahab's spies and for Paul, and the place of both judgment and open, unhidden prayer.
webster_full: WINDOW, n. 1. An opening in the wall of a building for the admission of light, and of air when necessary.
2. The word is from wind and eye, the Danish vindue, an opening through which the wind passes and the house looks out.
3. In Scripture, the windows of heaven; the openings through which rain is poured, used both of the flood and of abundant blessing. Gen. 7; Mal. 3.
4. A lattice; the ancient windows were closed with lattice work rather than with glass. Through the window she looked, and cried through the lattice. Judges 5.
5. Daniel's windows being open toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day; a testimony of prayer not concealed from adversaries. Dan. 6.
scriptures: Genesis 7:11

In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, the seventeenth day of the month, the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened.
Joshua 2:15
Then she let them down by a cord through the window: for her house was upon the town wall, and she dwelt upon the wall.
Malachi 3:10

Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.
Acts 20:9

And there sat in a window a certain young man named Eutychus, being fallen into a deep sleep: and as Paul was long preaching, he sunk down with sleep, and fell down from the third loft, and was taken up dead.
corruption_summary: Mal 3:10 has been detached from its covenant setting and turned into a formula of exchange, in which a payment triggers a guaranteed return of wealth — the one verse in Scripture where God says prove me, made into a lever.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity teaching rests more weight on this verse than on any other, and the misuse works by omission. Malachi is addressing a covenant nation under a covenant sanction: the whole nation was cursed with a curse because the whole nation had robbed God in tithes and offerings, and the storehouse is the temple storehouse that fed the Levites who had no inheritance. The promise of opened windows is the reversal of a national agricultural curse — the devourer rebuked, the vine not casting her fruit before the time. To lift it out and offer it to an individual as a guaranteed return on a donation is to promise what the text does not promise, and it consistently enriches the one collecting rather than the one giving.

What the passage does teach is worth keeping. God submits Himself to a test on the point of His people's giving, which He does nowhere else; He treats withheld offerings as robbery, which is a far graver category than stinginess; and the blessing He names is abundance beyond room to receive it. New Testament giving is not less than this but freer — every man according as he purposeth in his heart, not grudgingly or of necessity, for God loveth a cheerful giver — and it comes with the same assurance that God is able to make all grace abound. The difference is that the promise is of sufficiency for every good work, not of personal wealth on demand.
roots_summary: Hebrew challōn is the ordinary window of a house; 'arūbbâh is the lattice or sluice, the word in windows of heaven. Greek thuris, a diminutive of thura (door), is the New Testament term.
roots_lines: Hebrew challōn (H2474) — a window; the window of the ark, Rahab's window, Michal's window, and the window Jezebel looked out of.
Hebrew 'arūbbâh (H699) — a lattice, a sluice, a chimney; the word in the windows of heaven (Gen 7:11; Mal 3:10) and in the doves flying to their windows (Isa 60:8).
Hebrew eshnāb (H822) — a latticed window; used of Sisera's mother crying through the lattice (Jdg 5:28) and of the simple ones seen in Pro 7:6.
Greek thuris (G2376) — a window, little door; used only twice, of Paul let down through a window in a basket (2Co 11:33) and of Eutychus in the window at Troas.
Hebrew tsohar (H6672) — a light, an opening; the window commanded for the ark in Gen 6:16, a word otherwise meaning noon or brightness.
usage: Of the openings of heaven: the windows of heaven were opened (Gen 7:11); open you the windows of heaven (Mal 3:10); the LORD make windows in heaven (2Ki 7:2).
Of escape and deliverance: Rahab let them down by a cord through the window (Jos 2:15); Paul let down by the wall in a basket (Act 9:25).
Of what is seen or shewn through an opening: Michal looking through a window and despising David (2Sa 6:16); Daniel's windows open toward Jerusalem (Dan 6:10).

etymology: From Old French valee, from Latin vallis. The Hebrew is much richer than the English and distinguishes at least four things the Authorized Version renders alike: 'ēmeq, the broad open vale; gay', the narrow steep-sided ravine (the word in the valley of the son of Hinnom, whence Gehenna); biq'âh, a wide plain between mountains (the valley of dry bones); and nachal, a wadi, a torrent-bed dry for most of the year and dangerous in the rains.
biblical_def: In the geography of Scripture the valley is where the decisive things happen. It is the place of battle — the valley of Elah where David met Goliath, the valley of Jehoshaphat, the valley of Megiddo — because armies meet on level ground between the hills. It is the place of idolatry and judgment, since the valley of the son of Hinnom, where children were made to pass through the fire, gave its name to Gehenna, the standing New Testament word for hell. It is the place of vision and resurrection: the hand of the LORD set Ezekiel down “in the midst of the valley which was full of bones” (Eze 37:1), and there the question was asked whether these bones could live. It is the place of decision under the day of the LORD — “Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision” (Joe 3:14). Above all it is the shepherd's figure for the darkest passage of the believer's life: “Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me” (Psa 23:4). The preposition governs the comfort — through, not into; it is a passage and not a residence, and the presence of the shepherd rather than the absence of the shadow is what removes the fear. The prophetic reversal completes the theme: at the coming of the LORD “every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low” (Isa 40:4), the low places raised and the high brought down, which is the geography of grace stated as a landscape.
webster_summary: The low ground between hills; in Scripture the place of battle, of idolatrous fire, of the vision of dry bones and of decision under the day of the LORD, and, in the twenty-third psalm, the shadowed passage walked through rather than dwelt in, with the shepherd present.
webster_full: VALLEY, n. 1. A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.
2. In Scripture, the Hebrew has several words rendered by this one; the broad vale, the narrow ravine, the plain between mountains, and the torrent bed which is dry in summer.
3. The valley of the shadow of death; the darkest and most perilous passage of life, and by usage the approach of death itself. Psalm 23.

4. The valley of the son of Hinnom, or Tophet, where the idolatrous Israelites burnt their children to Molech, and which afterwards became the receptacle of the filth of the city; whence Gehenna, the word for hell. 2 Kings 23; Jer. 7.
5. The valley of decision; the place of judgment in the day of the LORD. Joel 3.
scriptures: Psalm 23:4
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
Ezekiel 37:1
The hand of the LORD was upon me, and carried me out in the spirit of the LORD, and set me down in the midst of the valley which was full of bones,
Joel 3:14
Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision: for the day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision.
Isaiah 40:4
Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain:
corruption_summary: The valley of the shadow of death is softened into a metaphor for a difficult season and emptied of both death and the shepherd, so that a psalm about dying in company becomes a sentiment about coping alone.
corruption_paragraphs: Psa 23:4 is the most quoted verse in the psalter and among the least attended. Two things are commonly lost. The first is death: the phrase is regularly applied to any hardship whatever, until the psalm no longer speaks to the one thing it was written to carry a man through. The second is the change of person. Through the first three verses David speaks of the shepherd in the third person — he maketh, he leadeth, he restoreth — and precisely at the valley he turns and speaks to Him: for thou art with me. The comfort of the psalm is not a proposition about God but the presence of God addressed directly, and it arrives exactly where the light fails. A reading that keeps the imagery and drops the Person has kept the wrapping.

The rod and the staff are the other casualty. Modern sentiment hears them as gentle accessories; they are a club and a crook, the one for beating off predators and the other for hooking a sheep out of a place it should not have gone. They comfort because they are instruments of force used on the sheep's behalf and, when needed, on the sheep. This is the same God who says that whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth. A shepherd who carried nothing would be no comfort at all in a ravine, and a God who never disciplined would be no Father.
roots_summary: Hebrew distinguishes the broad vale ('ēmeq), the steep ravine (gay'), the plain among mountains (biq'âh), and the seasonal torrent bed (nachal). Greek pharanx renders the term in Luke's quotation of Isaiah.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ēmeq (H6010) — a broad open valley or vale; the valley of Elah, the valley of Achor, the valley of Jehoshaphat.
Hebrew gay' (H1516) — a narrow steep-sided ravine; the word in the valley of the son of Hinnom and in the valley of the shadow of death (Psa 23:4).
Hebrew biq'âh (H1237) — a wide plain between mountains, from bāqa', to cleave; the plain of Shinar and the valley full of bones (Eze 37:1).
Hebrew nachal (H5158) — a torrent bed or wadi, dry in summer and flooding in the rains; the brook Kidron, the brook Cherith where Elijah was fed.
Greek pharanx (G5327) — a ravine, a valley; used in Luk 3:5, every valley shall be filled, quoting Isa 40:4 of the Baptist's ministry.
usage: Of battle and decision: the valley of Elah (1Sa 17:2); multitudes in the valley of decision (Joe 3:14).
Of judgment and idolatry: the valley of the son of Hinnom, Tophet (Jer 7:31-32), from which Gehenna takes its name.
Of the believer's dark passage and its reversal: through the valley of the shadow of death (Psa 23:4); every valley shall be exalted (Isa 40:4).

etymology: From Old French cort, from Latin cohors, an enclosure or yard and thence the company of people gathered in it — the same root that gives cohort. Both senses ride in the English word: a court is a walled open space, and a court is the retinue of a king. Hebrew chātsēr is the enclosed yard of the tabernacle and temple, and the word carries the plain sense of an enclosure with hangings around it.
biblical_def: The courts are the outer enclosure of God's house, and their whole doctrinal significance lies in their being outer. The tabernacle's court was a hundred cubits of fine twined linen hung on pillars (Exo 27:9), containing the brasen altar and the laver, and it was as far as the ordinary Israelite could come. Beyond it lay the holy place, where only priests entered, and the holiest of all, entered once a year by one man with blood. The court therefore taught access and its limits in the plainest possible architecture: you may come, and you may come this far, and there is a sacrifice standing between you and any nearer approach. Given that, the psalmists' language about the courts is astonishing in its warmth. “My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD” (Psa 84:2); a day in thy courts is better than a thousand; “Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise” (Psa 100:4). The blessedness of Psa 65:4 is expressly a chosen and caused approach — blessed is the man whom thou choosest, and causest to approach unto thee, that he may dwell in thy courts — which is election and effectual calling stated in the language of temple architecture. The New Testament completes it: the veil is rent, the way into the holiest is made manifest, and believers now have boldness to enter by the blood of Jesus. The longing of the psalmist for the court is answered by an access he did not have.
webster_summary: The walled outer enclosure of the tabernacle and temple, containing the altar and laver and marking the limit of the ordinary worshipper's approach; in the psalms the object of longing and thanksgiving, and the architectural picture of an access that Christ has since opened to the holiest itself.
webster_full: COURT, n. 1. A space inclosed by walls and open above, as before a house, or in the middle of a building.
2. In Scripture, the inclosed area of the tabernacle and of the temple. Thou shalt make the court of the tabernacle. Exod. 27.
3. The persons who compose the retinue of a prince or sovereign; whence the word is used both of the place and of the company assembled in it.
4. A place where justice is administered; the hall or chamber in which judges sit; and the judges themselves in session.
5. In the temple of Herod there were several courts; that of the Gentiles, that of the women, that of Israel, and that of the priests, each nearer than the last to the holy place.
scriptures: Psalm 84:2
My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD: my heart and my flesh crieth out for the living God.
Psalm 100:4
Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name.
Exodus 27:9
And thou shalt make the court of the tabernacle: for the south side southward there shall be hangings for the court of fine twined linen of an hundred cubits long for one side:
Psalm 65:4
Blessed is the man whom thou choosest, and causest to approach unto thee, that he may dwell in thy courts: we shall be satisfied with the goodness of thy house, even of thy holy temple.
corruption_summary: The graded courts are treated as a relic of primitive religion that the gospel simply abolished, so that the modern worshipper loses both the seriousness of approach and any sense that access to God cost anything.
corruption_paragraphs: The tabernacle's architecture was a sermon on the holiness of God, and where it is dismissed as mere ancient ritual the sermon is unpreached. The rending of the veil did not teach that the graded approach had always been an unnecessary severity; it taught that the barrier was real and that Christ had removed it at the cost of His flesh. Hebrews reasons precisely this way — the way into the holiest was not yet made manifest while the first tabernacle was standing — so the old arrangement is treated as a true statement of the problem, and the new as the true solution. A worship that has lost the courts tends to lose reverence first and then to lose the cross, since a God who was never inaccessible needed no one to open the way.

There is a corresponding error in the other direction, and it recurs whenever churches reintroduce graded holy space — a sanctuary the people may not enter, a table only clergy may approach, an altar rail treated as the boundary of the holy. The New Testament makes the whole congregation a holy priesthood with boldness to enter. To rebuild the partition in stone or in practice is to build again the thing Christ destroyed. The right recovery is neither the abolition of reverence nor the restoration of the veil, but the astonishment Hebrews expects: having therefore boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus…let us draw near.
roots_summary: Hebrew chātsēr is the enclosed yard of the sanctuary and also, in another sense, a settled village. Greek aulē covers the courtyard of a house or palace, the temple court, and the sheepfold.
roots_lines: Hebrew chātsēr (H2691) — a court, an enclosure; the court of the tabernacle and the courts of the LORD's house; the same form also denotes an unwalled village.
Hebrew 'āzārâh (H5835) — an enclosed space, a ledge or court; used of the courts of Ezekiel's temple and of the great court of 2Ch 4:9.
Greek aulē (G833) — a courtyard, palace court, fold; the high priest's palace where Peter denied the Lord (Mat 26:69), and the sheepfold of Joh 10:1.
Greek hieron (G2411) — the temple with its whole precinct and courts, as distinguished from naos, the sanctuary proper — a distinction the Authorized Version does not mark in English.
Greek parrhēsia (G3954) — boldness, freedom of speech and access; the word of Heb 10:19, the new standing that the old courts anticipated and could not give.
usage: Of the tabernacle and temple structure: the court of the tabernacle with its hangings of fine twined linen (Exo 27:9); the inner court and the great court (1Ki 6:36; 7:12).
Of the worshipper's longing and thanksgiving: my soul fainteth for the courts of the LORD (Psa 84:2); enter into his courts with praise (Psa 100:4).
Of a chosen and caused approach: blessed is the man whom thou choosest, and causest to approach unto thee (Psa 65:4).

etymology: From Latin tabula, a board or plank, and thence both a writing tablet and a board for eating. English keeps both senses and so does the Authorized Version, which speaks of the tables of stone written with the finger of God and of the table of shewbread — two different Hebrew words (lūach, a tablet; shulchān, a table for food) behind one English word. The second is the theologically loaded one: shulchān derives from a root meaning to send out or spread, a table being a spread thing.
biblical_def: To eat at a man's table in the ancient world was to be received by him, and Scripture builds a great deal on that fact. In the tabernacle the table of shittim wood overlaid with gold (Exo 25:23) held the shewbread, the bread of the Presence, twelve loaves for twelve tribes set continually before the LORD — a standing declaration that God keeps a table and His people are represented at it. David's psalm makes the table the emblem of confident provision in danger: “Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies” (Psa 23:5) — not a table after the enemies are gone, but a meal eaten unhurried while they watch. Mephibosheth, lame on both his feet, ate continually at the king's table, which is one of the clearest Old Testament pictures of adoption. The Canaanite woman argues from the table and wins her case — the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters' table (Mat 15:27) — and receives what she asked. In the New Testament the table becomes the Lord's: “Ye cannot be partakers of the Lord's table, and of the table of devils” (1Co 10:21), where the exclusivity is the whole point, since to eat at a table is to be in communion with the one who spreads it. Hence the Reformed practice of fencing the table, and hence the last promise: that ye may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom.
webster_summary: A board spread for food, and by extension the fellowship of those who eat at it; in Scripture the table of shewbread before the LORD, the table prepared in the presence of enemies, the king's table at which the lame are adopted, and the Lord's table which cannot be shared with the table of devils.
webster_full: TABLE, n. 1. A flat surface or plane, of some thickness; a board or plank supported by legs, on which provisions are set for eating.
2. Fare or entertainment of provisions; as, he keeps a good table. To eat at another's table is to be received into his house and friendship.
3. A tablet; a flat surface on which anything is written or engraved. The tables of stone written with the finger of God. Exod. 31.
4. In the tabernacle, the table of shewbread, overlaid with gold, on which twelve loaves were set in order before the LORD continually. Exod. 25; Levit. 24.
5. The Lord's table; the communion table, at which the supper is administered. Ye cannot be partakers of the Lord's table, and of the table of devils. 1 Cor. 10.
scriptures: Psalm 23:5
Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over.
1 Corinthians 10:21
Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord, and the cup of devils: ye cannot be partakers of the Lord's table, and of the table of devils.
Exodus 25:23
Thou shalt also make a table of shittim wood: two cubits shall be the length thereof, and a cubit the breadth thereof, and a cubit and a half the height thereof.
Matthew 15:27
And she said, Truth, Lord: yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters' table.
corruption_summary: The Lord's table is made either a bare memorial meal open to anyone present or a priestly sacrifice re-offered by a celebrant, and in both cases the apostolic warning against eating unworthily is treated as an embarrassment rather than as pastoral care.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome makes the table an altar and the supper a propitiatory sacrifice offered again by a priest, with the elements changed in substance. Hebrews forecloses this: by one offering He hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified, and where remission of sins is, there is no more offering for sin. The Lutheran account keeps the body and blood in, with, and under the elements; the bare memorialist keeps only a recollection. The Reformed confession holds the middle and gives up nothing — the signs remain bread and wine, and the believer by faith truly feeds on Christ crucified, who is really and spiritually present to His people by the Spirit. The table is a means of grace, not a bare reminder and not a repeated sacrifice.

The pastoral corruption is the abandonment of fencing. Paul says that he that eateth and drinketh unworthily eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body, and that for this cause many are weak and sickly. To invite all comers indiscriminately is not hospitality but negligence, since the warning is given for the communicant's protection. Equally, to fence the table so narrowly that troubled and self-suspecting Christians are driven away is to misuse it in the other direction; the supper is for sinners who repent and believe, and the examination Paul commands is self-examination, not the elders' inquisition. The table is the Lord's, and it is guarded because it is His and because those who come to it are His.
roots_summary: Hebrew shulchān is the table for food; lūach is the tablet of stone or wood. Greek trapeza, literally a four-footed thing, covers dining table, the Lord's table, and the moneychangers' counter; plax is the tablet.
roots_lines: Hebrew shulchān (H7979) — a table; some 71 occurrences, from the table of shewbread to Jezebel's prophets that ate at her table.
Hebrew lūach (H3871) — a tablet, board, plate; the tables of stone, and figuratively the table of the heart in Pro 3:3.
Hebrew lechem happānīm — the bread of the faces, rendered shewbread; the twelve loaves set on the table before the presence of the LORD continually.
Greek trapeza (G5132) — a table; used of the Lord's table (1Co 10:21), the tables of the moneychangers overthrown (Mat 21:12), and the daily serving of tables in Act 6:2.
Greek plax (G4109) — a flat tablet; the tables of the covenant in Heb 9:4, and the fleshy tables of the heart in 2Co 3:3.
usage: Of the sanctuary furniture: a table of shittim wood overlaid with pure gold (Exo 25:23-24), bearing the shewbread continually.
Of provision, welcome, and adoption: thou preparest a table before me (Psa 23:5); Mephibosheth did eat continually at the king's table (2Sa 9:13).
Of communion and its exclusivity: the Lord's table and the table of devils (1Co 10:21); that ye may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom (Luk 22:30).

etymology: From Old English pæþ, common West Germanic, a track worn by feet. The Hebrew words all carry the same idea of a way made by going: 'ōrach is a well-trodden road, nāthīb a beaten track, and ma'gāl literally a wagon-rut or the circular track worn round an encampment. A path in Scripture is therefore not an abstract direction but a groove — something previous feet have cut and present feet fall into.
biblical_def: The path is Scripture's standing figure for the settled course of a life, and it is treated as a matter of direction, illumination, and inheritance rather than of momentary choice. The shepherd leads “in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake” (Psa 23:3) — the paths are already righteous before the sheep is in them, and the reason given is the shepherd's reputation rather than the sheep's merit. Illumination is by the word: “Thou wilt shew me the path of life” (Psa 16:11), a psalm the apostles apply directly to the resurrection of Christ, so that the path of life is first His and then, in Him, ours. Guidance is by submission rather than by insight: “In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths” (Pro 3:6), where the promise attaches to acknowledgment, not to cleverness. And because a path is a groove worn by previous travellers, the prophet's counsel is retrospective: “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls” (Jer 6:16). The verse ends with the refusal that makes it a judgment oracle — But they said, We will not walk therein — and that refusal, not ignorance, is the usual reason men are lost. Scripture also speaks of paths that are crooked, of the path of the wicked which is as darkness, and of the just whose path is as the shining light that shineth more and more unto the perfect day.
webster_summary: A track worn by the feet of those who have gone before; in Scripture the settled course of a life, led by the shepherd in righteousness, lighted by the word, directed by acknowledgment of God, and found by asking for the old paths rather than by devising new ones.
webster_full: PATH, n. 1. A way beaten or trodden by the feet of man or beast; a track, or way formed by treading or walking.
2. Course of life; the manner in which a man walks. He leadeth me in the paths of righteousness. Psalm 23.
3. Course of providence, or of divine dealing. All the paths of the LORD are mercy and truth unto such as keep his covenant. Psalm 25.
4. Precepts; rule of conduct. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path. Psalm 119.
5. The old paths; the ways of the fathers, and of the word of God, as distinguished from the new ways of men's devising. Jer. 6.
scriptures: Psalm 23:3
He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake.
Psalm 16:11
Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
Proverbs 3:6
In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
Jeremiah 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
corruption_summary: The path has been privatised: the biblical figure of a trodden way received from those who went before is replaced by the modern conviction that each man must find his own path, which is precisely the counsel Jer 6:16 records as refused.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant modern usage of the word is self-referential — my path, your path, the path that is right for you — and it assumes that authenticity is the test and that a way received from others is by definition inauthentic. Scripture's figure runs the opposite direction. A path is worn by feet that came first; it is inherited, and its trustworthiness is established by where it has already led. Jeremiah's counsel is to stand, look, ask for the old paths, identify the good way among them, and then walk. Every verb in that sequence is an act of submission to something outside the self, and the promise attached is the one modern autonomy most conspicuously fails to deliver: ye shall find rest for your souls.

This is not a defence of mere traditionalism, and Jeremiah does not offer one. He does not say every old path is good; he says ask where the good way is among them, which requires discernment and a standard. The standard is the word, which is the lamp to the feet and the light to the path — near light for the next step and general light for the road. The Reformed instinct here is exactly right: the confessions and the fathers are consulted seriously as those who walked before us, and they are never authoritative over Scripture. What is refused is the notion that a man in his own generation, with his own lights, is competent to cut a new track through country he has never seen.
roots_summary: Hebrew has several words for a trodden way: 'ōrach (a well-worn road), nāthīb (a beaten track), and ma'gāl (a wagon rut or entrenchment). Greek tribos likewise names a way worn by rubbing and treading.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ōrach (H734) — a way, path, road; used of the path of the just that shineth more and more (Pro 4:18) and of the paths of the LORD which are mercy and truth.
Hebrew nāthīb (H5410) — a beaten track; the word in Psa 119:105, a light unto my path, and in Job's question about the path no fowl knoweth.
Hebrew ma'gāl (H4570) — a wagon track, an entrenchment, a rut; the paths of righteousness of Psa 23:3 and the paths of Pro 4:26, ponder the path of thy feet.
Hebrew derek (H1870) — way, road, manner of life; the broader term standing behind the two ways of Psa 1 and the good way of Jer 6:16.
Greek tribos (G5147) — a worn path, a beaten way; used in the Baptist's summons, make his paths straight (Mat 3:3), quoting Isa 40:3.
usage: Of the course in which God leads: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness (Psa 23:3); all the paths of the LORD are mercy and truth (Psa 25:10).
Of guidance and illumination: he shall direct thy paths (Pro 3:6); a light unto my path (Psa 119:105); thou wilt shew me the path of life (Psa 16:11).
Of the inherited way and its refusal: ask for the old paths (Jer 6:16); the path of the just is as the shining light (Pro 4:18); the way of the wicked is as darkness (Pro 4:19).

etymology: From Old English strāt, borrowed from Latin strata (via), a paved way — literally a strewn or laid road, from sternere, to spread out. The Hebrew r'chōb is not a narrow lane but a broad place, from a root meaning wide — the open square inside the gate where markets were held, elders sat, and the assembly gathered. Greek plateia is the same idea: the broad way, as distinguished from rhumē, the narrow lane.
biblical_def: The street in Scripture is public space, and it is where a society's true condition becomes visible. It is the place of proclamation: “Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets” (Pro 1:20) — personified Wisdom does not wait in a school but calls in the open square where the crowd is, so that no one may plead that he was never told. It is the place of the gospel's reach to the excluded, since when the invited guests refused, the master said, “Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in hither the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind” (Luk 14:21). It is the place of ordinary providence and specific address, as when the Lord directed Ananias to “the street which is called Straight” (Act 9:11) to find a named man in a named house, praying. It is also the measure of a city's ruin or peace — Jerusalem's desolation is pictured by streets where the young children faint, and her restoration by old men and old women dwelling in the streets of Jerusalem with the streets full of boys and girls playing in them. The last use crowns the theme: “the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass” (Rev 21:21), and through the midst of that street runs the river of water of life, with the tree of life on either side. The material men grasp at and pave nothing with is what the city of God walks on.
webster_summary: The public way and open square of a city; in Scripture the place where wisdom cries aloud, where the gospel's invitation reaches the poor and maimed, where a city's ruin or peace is displayed, and, in the new Jerusalem, a thoroughfare of pure gold with the river of life running through it.
webster_full: STREET, n. 1. Properly, a paved way or road; but in usage, any way or road in a city, chiefly a main way, in distinction from a lane or alley.
2. In Scripture, the Hebrew word denotes rather a broad place or open square, especially that within the gate, where the people assembled and the elders sat in judgment.
3. The place of public concourse, and hence of public proclamation. Wisdom uttereth her voice in the streets. Prov. 1.
4. Figuratively, the state of a city's peace or desolation. The streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in the streets thereof. Zech. 8.
5. The street of the new Jerusalem, described as pure gold, as it were transparent glass, with the river of water of life proceeding through the midst of it. Rev. 21, 22.
scriptures: Proverbs 1:20
Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets:
Luke 14:21

So that servant came, and shewed his lord these things. Then the master of the house being angry said to his servant, Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in hither the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind.
Acts 9:11
And the Lord said unto him, Arise, and go into the street which is called Straight, and enquire in the house of Judas for one called Saul, of Tarsus: for, behold, he prayeth,
Revelation 21:21
And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl: and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass.
corruption_summary: The public square is claimed as a religiously neutral space from which the church must withdraw, though Scripture makes the street precisely where wisdom cries aloud and where the invitation is carried to those who will never come otherwise.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine that faith is a private matter with no proper voice in public places is comparatively recent and is not neutral. Someone always speaks in the square; the question is only who. Proverbs pictures Wisdom crying in the chief place of concourse, in the openings of the gates, and the reason is stated: how long, ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity? The public call exists because the people who most need it will not seek it out. Israel's prophets stood in the gate; the apostles preached in the market at Athens and disputed daily in the school of Tyrannus; and the Lord Himself taught in the temple courts and on the open hillside. A church that accepts confinement to its own premises has conceded a claim the Scriptures do not grant.

The Lord's own guard against the opposite error must be kept in the same hand. He warns against those who love to pray standing in the corners of the streets that they may be seen of men, and against sounding a trumpet in the streets when giving alms. The street is the place of proclamation, not of display — the difference being whether the aim is that men should hear the message or should notice the messenger. Both the withdrawal and the performance fail the same test, and the parable of the great supper settles what the street is actually for: it is where the servant goes, at his master's command and in some haste, to bring in those who would not otherwise be at the table.
roots_summary: Hebrew r'chōb is the broad open place within the gate, from a root meaning wide; chūts is what is outside, the street as opposed to the house. Greek plateia is the broad way, rhumē the narrow lane; Luk 14:21 uses both together.
roots_lines: Hebrew r'chōb (H7339) — a broad open place, the square within the gate; from rāchab, to be wide. The place of assembly, of judgment, and of public reading of the law (Neh 8:1).
Hebrew chūts (H2351) — the outside, that which is without; rendered street where the contrast with indoors is in view, as in Wisdom crying without (Pro 1:20).
Greek plateia (G4113) — a broad way, a street; the feminine of platus, wide — the same adjective as the broad way that leadeth to destruction (Mat 7:13).
Greek rhumē (G4505) — a narrow lane or alley; paired with plateia in Luk 14:21, streets and lanes, so that neither the wide nor the narrow is left uncanvassed.
Greek amphodon (G296) — a road round, a street corner or block; used in Mar 11:4, the colt tied by the door without in a place where two ways met.
usage: Of public proclamation: Wisdom uttereth her voice in the streets (Pro 1:20); he shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street (Isa 42:2), said of the Servant's manner.
Of the gospel's reach and of ordinary providence: go out quickly into the streets and lanes (Luk 14:21); the street which is called Straight (Act 9:11).
Of a city's desolation or peace: they that did feed delicately are desolate in the streets (Lam 4:5); the streets full of boys and girls playing (Zec 8:5); the street of pure gold (Rev 21:21).
